Paul Kagame: President of Rwanda since 2000. The RPF was one of the main belligerents of the Rwandan Civil War and was the armed force which ended the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
The first Kerala Chief Minister to win re-election after completing a full term, this CPI(M) leader represented the Dharmadom constituency — who is he?
Which Chinese diplomat rocketed to foreign minister in December 2022, then vanished from public view six months later and was quietly removed by July 2023?
Also known as Calvinism, this 16th-century Protestant branch stresses biblical authority, God's sovereignty, and covenant theology as articulated by John Calvin — what movement is this?
Nicknamed 'Captain Comeback,' this Naval Academy grad won the 1963 Heisman Trophy, served a tour in Vietnam, then led the Dallas Cowboys to two Super Bowl titles — who is he?
Roger Staubach: American football player and Navy officer (born 1942)

As students in 1930s Paris, this Syrian and Michel Aflaq cooked up a doctrine blending nationalism and socialism, then co-founded the Ba'ath Party — and decades later he was assassinated in Paris. Who is it?
Sparked when Qing officials seized a British-registered ship called the Arrow in 1856, this conflict between Britain, France, and China forced the legalization of the drug trade — which conflict?
Second Opium War: 1856–1860 war between British–French forces and China.
In 1968 she became the first Black woman elected to the U.S. Congress, and in 1972 the first Black major-party presidential candidate — who was she?
Formed after the October Revolution of 1917 and dissolved in 1991, this Moscow-based superpower was the largest country on Earth by area — which one?
Soviet Union: Country in Eurasia from 1922 to 1991.
Born to a Cossack family in Poltava, this journalist-turned-revolutionary became Supreme Commander of the Ukrainian People's Army during the Ukrainian War of Independence — who was he?
Serving as Dachau's second commandant and later the first inspector of Nazi concentration camps, this SS commander was killed in 1943 when his plane was shot down over Kharkov — who was he?
Grand Duke Konstantin Pavlovich of Russia
This Japanese term describes marginalized, often homeless youth — a mix of runaways and those seeking community after bullying — who gather in Kabukicho's back alleys. What is this subculture called?
Toyoko kids: Youth group in Tokyo, Japan.
Composed in an archaic Sanskrit dialect, this collection of four ancient hymn texts forms the oldest layer of Hindu scripture — what are they collectively called?
This Warring States-era Chinese general commanded conquests of three rival kingdoms and is remembered by tradition as one of the four greatest generals of the late Warring States period — who was he?
Wang Jian (Qin): 3rd century BC Chinese military general.
Famous for pioneering sensationalist 'yellow journalism,' this publisher fought a fierce circulation war against Joseph Pulitzer's New York paper after acquiring a rival New York daily — who was he?
William Randolph Hearst: American newspaper publisher (1863–1951)
A former Palmach commando, this Israeli general became the first prime minister born in the region of Palestine — and was assassinated while serving a second term in 1995. Who was he?
Yitzhak Rabin: Prime Minister of Israel (1974–1977; 1992–1995)
A dispute between two rival lords escalated into a decade-long Japanese civil war from 1467 to 1477 that triggered the Warring States period — what was this conflict called?
Ōnin War: 15th-century civil war in Japan.
Which one below was born first?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four. Qian received his undergraduate education in mechanical engineering at National Chiao Tung University in Shanghai in 1934.
Which of these four was born earliest?
Emanuel Swedenborg (born 1688) is the earliest of the four. Swedenborg had a prolific career as an inventor and scientist.
Which one below was born first?
Levi Strauss (born 1829) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four came first?
C++ (founded 1983) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the astronomer from these four.
Jane Luu is an astronomer. Luu (Vietnamese: Lưu Lệ Hằng; born July 1963) is a Vietnamese-American astronomer and defense systems engineer.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Jim Simons is a mathematician. James Harris Simons (April 25, 1938 – May 10, 2024) was an American hedge fund manager, investor, mathematician, and philanthropist.
What is the atomic number of Niobium?
Niobium is a chemical element; it has symbol Nb (formerly columbium, Cb) and atomic number 41.
What is the atomic number of Phosphorus?
Phosphorus is a chemical element; it has symbol P and atomic number 15.
In what year was Émile Durkheim born?
Émile Durkheim: David Émile Durkheim (French: [emil dyʁkɛm] or [dyʁkajm]; 15 April 1858 – 15 November 1917) was a French sociologist.
In what year was Gregor Mendel born?
Gregor Mendel: Mendel worked with seven characteristics of pea plants: plant height, pod shape and colour, seed shape and colour, and flower position and colour.
In what year was Leonhard Euler born?
Leonhard Euler: Euler has been called a "universal genius" who "was fully equipped with almost unlimited powers of imagination, intellectual gifts and extraordinary memory".
In what year did Alexander Hamilton die?
Alexander Hamilton: Born out of wedlock in Charlestown on the Caribbean island of Nevis, Hamilton was orphaned as a child and taken in by a prosperous merchant.
In what year did Kitty O'Neil die?
Kitty O'Neil: O'Neil subsequently moved into car racing and became a pioneering woman in the stunt industry in Hollywood.
In what year was Huntington's disease discovered?
Huntington's disease (HD), also known as Huntington's chorea, is a fatal neurodegenerative disease that is usually inherited.
Swift (programming language): Apple Inc. Swift compiles to machine code and uses an LLVM-based compiler.
Levofloxacin: Pfizer. Levofloxacin, sold under the brand name Levaquin among others, is a broad-spectrum antibiotic of the fluoroquinolone drug class.
Publishing: Germany. It has various divisions such as trade/retail publishing of fiction and non-fiction, educational publishing, and academic and scientific publishing.
Who is credited with discovering Glutathione?
Glutathione: Frederick Hopkins. Glutathione (GSH,) is a tripeptide made of the amino acids glutamate, cysteine, and glycine.
Who is credited with discovering Blockchain?
Blockchain: Satoshi Nakamoto. A blockchain is a distributed ledger with growing lists of records (blocks) that are securely linked together via cryptographic hashes.
Who is credited with discovering Ethology?
Ethology: Isidore Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire. Ethology is a branch of zoology that studies the behaviour of non-human animals.
Sitting atop the kidneys, this pair of endocrine glands produces hormones including adrenaline, aldosterone, and cortisol. What organ is it?
Adrenal gland (also known as suprarenal glands) are endocrine glands that produce a variety of hormones including adrenaline and the steroids aldosterone and cortisol.
Formed naturally around volcanic vents and on burning coal dumps, this soluble white crystalline salt serves as both a fertilizer and a food additive — what's the compound with formula NH4Cl?
Ammonium chloride is an inorganic chemical compound with the chemical formula NH4Cl, also written as Cl.
This emotion is defined by dread over events that haven't happened yet, distinguishing it from fear, which responds to a threat that's already present. What is it?
Anxiety is an emotion characterized by an unpleasant state of inner turmoil and includes feelings of dread over anticipated events.

A professor at the University of North Carolina, this molecular biologist co-founded a foundation supporting Turkish students while researching DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, and circadian rhythms — who is he?
Aziz Sancar (born 8 September 1946) is a Turkish-American molecular biologist specializing in DNA repair, cell cycle checkpoints, and circadian clock.
Before TV stardom he was a Boeing mechanical engineer who invented a hydraulic resonance suppressor tube for 747s, then jumped to sketch comedy on Almost Live! — which science communicator?
Bill Nye (born November 27, 1955) is an American science communicator, television presenter, and former mechanical engineer.
One of the largest, longest-lived trees in the Amazon, this species produces a fruit and shell weighing up to two kilograms, with edible seeds famed for their selenium content — what tree is it?
Brazil nut (Bertholletia excelsa) refers to a South American tree of the monotypic genus Bertholletia in the family Lecythidaceae as well as the tree's commercially-harvested edible seeds.

Spread through contact with infected feces and capable of killing up to 91% of untreated cases, this highly contagious virus mainly strikes dogs and wolves but can also infect foxes, cats, and skunks — what's the virus?
Canine parvovirus (also referred to as CPV, CPV2, or parvo) is a contagious virus mainly affecting dogs and wolves.
This English polymath is credited with inventing the first mechanical computer and designing an unrealized 'analytical engine' programmed using ideas borrowed from the Jacquard loom. Who is he?
Charles Babbage (26 December 1791 - 18 October 1871) was an English polymath.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Derived from Greek words meaning universe and study of, this scientific and philosophical field examines the nature of existence at the grandest scale — what is it called?
Cosmology (from Ancient Greek (cosmos) 'the universe, the world' and - (logia) 'study of') is the study of the nature of the universe, the cosmos.
Specialists in this branch of medicine handle skin infections, cancers, hair loss, and cosmetic concerns, sometimes even life-threatening conditions like severe burns — which medical field?
Dermatology is the branch of medicine dealing with the skin.
A German-born British economist, he championed human-scale, appropriate technology in a hugely influential 1973 book ranked among the 100 most important since WWII — who is he?

E. F. Schumacher (16 August 1911 - 4 September 1977) was a German-born British statistician and economist who is best known for his proposals for human-scale, decentralised and appropriate technologies.

This genus's tapering spacing of stem nodes toward the tip is credited with inspiring John Napier's work on logarithms; today it's the sole living genus of an ancient, spore-producing plant lineage nicknamed horsetail — which genus?
Equisetum (horsetail) is the only living genus in Equisetaceae, a family of vascular plants that reproduce by spores rather than seeds.

Patented in 1979 but not used medically until 1996, this second-generation antihistamine treats allergic rhinitis and hives while causing far less drowsiness than older allergy medications — what's the drug?
Fexofenadine is an antihistamine medication used in the treatment of allergy symptoms such as allergic rhinitis and urticaria.
Reclassified twice before settling into its own genus, this Gram-variable, non-spore-forming coccobacillus is barely one to 1.5 micrometers across — which species?
Gardnerella vaginalis is a species of Gram-variable-staining facultative anaerobic bacteria.
This system of rules governs how a language is structured, covering everything from word order to the deeper study of sounds, meaning, and sentence formation — what is it called?
Grammar is the system of rules that governs how a natural language is structured and used, as evidenced by its speakers or writers.
Living to the age of 104, this French pioneer of algebraic topology was also the son-in-law of physicist Pierre Weiss and the eldest of a remarkable scientific brood — who was he?
Henri Cartan (8 July 1904 - 13 August 2008) was a French mathematician who made substantial contributions to algebraic topology.
Often caused by kidney failure or certain blood-pressure medications, this condition means too much potassium in the blood, with levels above 5.5 mmol/L — what's it called?
Hyperkalemia is an elevated level of potassium (K+) in the blood.
This mild oxidizing agent and Lewis acid, with the formula FeCl3, is commonly used to purify water and to etch metal surfaces — which compound is it?
Iron(III) chloride is an inorganic compound with the formula FeCl3. The anhydrous derivative is a Lewis acid, while all forms are mild oxidizing agents.

A civil engineer who commanded the Australian Corps in 1918, this WWI general was called by historian A. J. P. Taylor 'the only general of creative originality produced by the First World War' — who was he?
John Monash (27 June 1865 - 8 October 1931) was an Australian military commander of the First World War and a civil engineer.
This fatal prion disease, once common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, was nicknamed 'laughing sickness' and spread through ritual funerary cannibalism. What is it?
Kuru (disease) was a rare, incurable, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was formerly common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea.

This Finnish-American software engineer has led development of a hugely popular open-source operating system kernel since 1991, and also created the distributed version-control system Git — who is he?
Linus Torvalds (born 28 December 1969) is a Finnish and American software engineer who is the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991.
This naturally occurring white solid, found as the mineral brucite, has very low water solubility and is a key ingredient in a well-known antacid remedy — what is it?
Magnesium hydroxide is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Mg(OH)2.
First made in 1955 by bombarding einsteinium with alpha particles, this synthetic element 101 is named for the father of the periodic table — what is it?
Mendelevium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Md (formerly Mv) and atomic number 101.
These cylindrical, burrowing insects have small eyes and shovel-like front limbs highly adapted for digging underground — name the family?
Mole cricket are members of the insect family Gryllotalpidae, in the order Orthoptera (grasshoppers, locusts, and crickets).
In this category of over 80 recognized conditions, the body's adaptive immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissue as though it were foreign. What is it?

Navel (clinically known as the umbilicus; pl.: umbilici or umbilicuses; also known as the belly button or tummy button) is a protruding, flat, or hollowed area on the abdomen at the attachment site of the umbilical cord.
Despite counting the killer whale and pilot whale among its roughly forty species, this marine mammal family is more closely related to porpoises than to true whales — what family is it?
Oceanic dolphin are a widely distributed family of dolphins that live in the sea.

Nicknamed the 'white rats' of its phylum for how often it's used in classroom and lab experiments, this single-celled ciliate thrives in freshwater, brackish, and marine habitats — what organism is it?
Paramecium ((ee-)m, -see-m, plural "paramecia" only when used as a vernacular name) is a genus of eukaryotic, unicellular ciliates, widespread in freshwater, brackish, and marine environments.

This cellular process, in which a cell's outer membrane engulfs a large particle to form an internal compartment, is a key immune-system mechanism for clearing pathogens and cellular debris — what is it called?

Phagocytosis (from Ancient Greek (phagein) 'to eat' and (kytos) 'cell') is the process by which a cell uses its plasma membrane to engulf a large particle (0.5 m), giving rise to an internal compartment called the phagosome.
Carrying minor-planet number 134340, this icy Kuiper-belt world has about one-sixth the Moon's mass and got demoted when astronomers rewrote the rules — what is it?
Pluto (minor-planet number 134340) is a dwarf planet in the Kuiper belt, a ring of bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune.
Unfolding inside every cell in two acts called transcription and translation, this process turns a gene's DNA into messenger RNA on its way to building enzymes and hormones — what is it?
Protein biosynthesis is a core biological process, occurring inside cells, balancing the loss of cellular proteins (via degradation or export) through the production of fresh proteins.
A canine native to the southeastern United States, intermediate in size between the coyote and gray wolf. For a century its taxonomic classification has been contentious. What is it?
Red wolf (Canis rufus) is a canine native to the southeastern United States.
Mostly used in wear-resistant electrical contacts and thick-film resistors, which rare, chemically unreactive platinum-group metal has atomic number 44?
Ruthenium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ru and atomic number 44.

Native only to groves on California's Sierra Nevada slopes, this conifer species includes the largest trees on Earth by volume, though fewer than 80,000 remain and it's now listed as endangered — what's the species?

Sequoiadendron giganteum (also known as the giant sequoia, giant redwood, Sierra redwood or Wellingtonia) is a species of coniferous tree, classified in the family Cupressaceae in the subfamily Sequoioideae.
Called sun spiders, camel spiders, and wind scorpions, these dry-climate arachnids are neither true spiders nor scorpions, and urban legends wildly exaggerate their danger — what order are they?
Solifugae is an order of arachnids known variously as solifuges, sun spiders, camel spiders, wind scorpions, and jerrymanders.
Generated in mitochondria via the TCA cycle, this dicarboxylic compound gets converted into fumarate by an enzyme that helps build ATP — which molecule?
Succinic acid is a dicarboxylic acid with the chemical formula (CH2)2(CO2H)2.
Known pharmaceutically as dronabinol, this is the principal psychoactive compound found in cannabis, used medically to relieve chemotherapy-induced nausea. What compound is it?
Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) is a cannabinoid found in cannabis.
Following the instructions of the genetic code, which cellular process decodes mRNA outside the nucleus to assemble a polypeptide chain?
Translation (biology) is the process in biological cells in which proteins are produced using RNA molecules as templates.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
This biological process unfolds in predictable phases — hemostasis, inflammation, cell proliferation, and tissue remodeling — to replace damaged skin after the barrier is broken. What is it?
Wound healing refers to a living organism's replacement of destroyed or damaged tissue by newly produced tissue.
This mucolytic drug is the go-to antidote for acetaminophen overdose, working by boosting glutathione to neutralize the drug's toxic byproducts — what is it?
Acetylcysteine: Medication used to treat overdose of paracetamol.
Twice President of the Swiss Confederation, this Social Democratic politician left the Federal Council in 2023 to become Secretary General of the Council of Europe — who is he?
Alain Berset: Swiss Federal Councillor from 2012 to 2023.

Native to South Africa's Western Cape, this flowering bulb genus lends its common name to popular winter houseplants that actually belong to a different genus, Hippeastrum — which bulb, also called the naked lady or Jersey lily?
Amaryllis: Genus of plants. Amaryllis is the only genus in the subtribe Amaryllidinae (tribe Amaryllideae).
Named from Greek words for 'curved' and 'vertebra,' this type of arthritis causes long-term inflammation where the spine meets the pelvis — what is it?
Ankylosing spondylitis: Type of arthritis of the spine. Ankylosing spondylitis (AS) is a type of arthritis from the disease spectrum of axial spondyloarthritis.
The fourth-brightest star in the night sky and the brightest in the northern hemisphere, this aging red giant in Boötes has ballooned to 25 times the Sun's size despite sharing its mass — what is it?
Arcturus: Brightest star in the constellation Boötes. It has the Bayer designation α Boötis, which is Latinized to Alpha Boötis and abbreviated Alpha Boo or α Boo.

Also called the moon jellyfish, this once-thought-cosmopolitan species was split into roughly 28 separate species in the 2020s and is now known to live only in the north Atlantic and off Argentina — which species?
Aurelia aurita: Species of jellyfish. The species now identified as A. aurita is only found in the north Atlantic and in Argentina, and is not dangerous to humans.

This single-engine turboprop trainer, a license-built version of the Swiss Pilatus PC-9, replaced America's Cessna 'Tweet' and Turbo Mentor trainers in the 2010s and flies under the nickname 'Efroni' in Israel — which aircraft?
Beechcraft T-6 Texan II: Single-engine, low-wing tandem-seat turboprop military training aircraft.
This flowering vine's dried fruit is one of the most commonly traded spices in the world, its heat coming from a compound called piperine — what plant?
Black pepper: Ground fruit of the family Piperaceae.

Commonly known as mad cow disease, this fatal neurodegenerative illness in cattle is caused by a misfolded prion and can spread to humans as a variant of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What is this cattle disease called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy: Fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle. The United Kingdom was afflicted with an outbreak of BSE and vCJD in the 1980s and 1990s.
Jointly developed by Pakistan and China as a lightweight fourth-generation fighter meant to eventually succeed the F-16 in Pakistan's air force, this jet's Chinese designation is FC-1 — what is it?
CAC/PAC JF-17 Thunder: Sino-Pakistani multirole fighter aircraft.
This medical emergency occurs when the heart suddenly stops beating effectively, cutting off blood flow to the brain and other organs within minutes — what is it called?
Cardiac arrest: Sudden or unexpected loss of heartbeat.
Latin for 'little brain,' this hindbrain structure fine-tunes motor coordination and timing without actually initiating movement — what is it?
Cerebellum: Structure at the rear of the vertebrate brain, beneath the cerebrum.
Every animal cell makes this waxy sterol — the liver most of all — and it doubles as the raw material for steroid hormones, bile acids, and vitamin D. What is it?
Cholesterol: Sterol biosynthesized by all animal cells.
This scale insect that feeds on prickly pear cacti produces carminic acid, the basis of the red dye carmine used in lipstick and food coloring — what is it?
Cochineal: Species of insect producing the crimson dye carmine.
Known historically as blue vitriol, this bright blue crystalline compound with the formula CuSO4 forms an octahedral complex when dissolved in water — what compound?
Copper(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. It forms hydrates CuSO4·nH2O, where n can range from 1 to 7.

Named from the Greek for "dark blue," this compound's signature group is a carbon atom triple-bonded to nitrogen — and its soluble salts, like the potassium and sodium versions, are infamously deadly. What is it?
Cyanide: Any molecule with a cyano group (C≡N)
Working alongside longtime colleague Ken Thompson, this American computer scientist co-created the Unix operating system and the C programming language — who is he?
Dennis Ritchie: American computer scientist known for Unix (1941–2011)
Made from a fermented batter of rice and black gram, which thin, savoury South Indian flatbread is traditionally served with chutney and sambar?
Dosa (food): Thin batter bread originating from South India.
Element 99 was first discovered in the radioactive debris of the very first hydrogen bomb explosion in 1952 — what synthetic actinide is it?
Einsteinium: Chemical element with atomic number 99 (Es)
Named from the Latin word for hedgehog, this mammal family unites spiny Eurasian and African hedgehogs with their Southeast Asian cousins, the moonrats — which family?
Erinaceidae: Family of mammals. Erinaceidae (from Latin erinaceus, "hedgehog") is a family in the order Eulipotyphla, consisting of the hedgehogs and moonrats.

Nicknamed the 'yaffle' for its loud call, this bird has a bright red crown and a black moustache stripe, and feeds mostly on ants on the ground rather than drumming on trees like its relatives — what is it?

European green woodpecker: Species of bird. It is resident across much of Europe and the western Palearctic but in Spain and Portugal it is replaced by the similar Iberian green woodpecker (Picus sharpei).
Also known as the bodhi tree, this species is revered in four South Asian religions as the tree beneath which Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment — which species?
Ficus religiosa: Species of fig. Ficus religiosa or sacred fig is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to Moraceae, the fig or mulberry family.

One of the first management consultants, this American mechanical engineer wrote a 1909 book — later voted the most influential management book of the 20th century — and helped found industrial engineering. Who was he?
Frederick Winslow Taylor: American mechanical engineer (1856–1915)
Combining Greek words for 'earth,' 'form,' and 'study,' what field examines how landscapes and seafloor features form and evolve over time?
With DNA up to 99% identical to ours, this troop-dwelling great ape — led by a dominant 'silverback' — is the largest living primate on Earth — what is it?
Gorilla: Genus of large African apes.
First described in 1893 during a flu pandemic and mistakenly blamed as its cause, this Gram-negative bacterium causes pneumonia and meningitis mainly in infants — which bacterium?
Haemophilus influenzae: Species of bacterium. The bacteria are mesophilic and grow best at temperatures between 35 and 37 °C.
Introduced to Britain in the 19th century as an ornamental plant, this Caucasus-native's sap causes painful blistering burns when exposed skin meets sunlight — which species?
Heracleum mantegazzianum: Species of flowering plant. Heracleum mantegazzianum, commonly known as giant hogweed, is a monocarpic perennial herbaceous plant in the carrot family Apiaceae.

In the Renaissance this field of study covered classical literature and language rather than religion or divinity, and today it groups subjects using critical and interpretive methods rather than empirical ones — what broad academic category is this?
Humanities: Academic disciplines that study society and culture.

Dubbed the 'saviour of mothers,' this Hungarian doctor proved in 1847 that hand-washing with chlorinated lime solutions could drastically cut deadly childbed fever at a Vienna maternity clinic — who is he?
Ignaz Semmelweis: Early pioneer of antiseptic procedures.
Native to South America but planted worldwide for its long-lasting violet blooms, this tree — also called the black poui — is listed as Vulnerable in its wild range by the IUCN. What is it?
Jacaranda mimosifolia: Species of sub-tropical tree.
This British physicist shared the 1951 Nobel Prize with Ernest Walton for first splitting the atomic nucleus — a feat that opened the way to nuclear power and weapons. Who was he?
Defined by a carbon-oxygen double bond flanked by two carbon groups, this class of organic compound includes acetone and gives some sugars and steroids like testosterone their structure — what is it?
Ketone: Organic compounds of the form >C=O.
A genus of 47 flowering plant species in the sage family, prized for its fragrant oil and used in traditional medicine, cosmetics, and as a culinary herb across Mediterranean climates — which genus?
Lavandula: Genus of plants. Lavandula (common name lavender) is a genus of 47 known species of perennial flowering plants in the sage family, Lamiaceae.
Soft, movable, and painless, this benign fatty-tissue growth most often shows up under the skin on the upper back, shoulders, or abdomen — what is it?
Lipoma: Benign tumor made of fat tissue.
Native to China, Japan, Korea and Nepal and blooming in late summer after heavy rainfall, this plant's alternate names include the hurricane lily and the corpse flower — what is it?
Lycoris radiata: Species of plant. It is originally from China, Japan, Korea and Nepal and spread from there to the United States and elsewhere.
This American cultural anthropologist's 1928 fieldwork, Coming of Age in Samoa, made her a household name for exploring adolescence and sexuality in Pacific societies — who is she?
Typically occurring between ages 45 and 55, this natural decline in estrogen and progesterone permanently ends a woman's menstrual periods?
Menopause: Time when menstrual periods stop permanently.

Soviet pilots called it the "Balalaika" because its planform looked like the stringed instrument, while Poles dubbed it "Ołówek" — the pencil — for its slender fuselage; which most-produced supersonic jet in history earned all those nicknames?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-21: 1956 Soviet fighter aircraft family.
Drawn from the latex of opium poppies, this naturally occurring opiate acts straight on the central nervous system to dull pain — but risks dependence and tolerance. What is it?
Morphine: Pain medication of the opiate family.
This chronic neurological disorder scrambles the sleep-wake cycle, bringing on excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep paralysis, and sudden episodes of muscle collapse called cataplexy — what is it?
Narcolepsy: Human sleep disorder. Narcolepsy is a chronic neurological disorder that impairs the ability to regulate sleep–wake cycles, and specifically impacts REM (rapid eye movement) sleep.

Usually made from unleavened dough that's rolled, cut, or extruded into long strips, this staple food is called pasta in Italian cuisine and split into wheat-based and starch-based varieties in Chinese cooking — what is it?
Noodle: Staple food made from unleavened dough, commonly long and thin.

Born out of military planning before World War II, this branch of applied mathematics uses optimization and statistics to find the best possible outcome for real-world decisions — what field, sometimes called management science?
Operations research: Discipline concerning the application of advanced analytical methods.
Also called the corn poppy or Flanders poppy, this red flowering weed has symbolized remembrance in the Commonwealth since World War I — what plant is it?
Papaver rhoeas: Species of flowering plant in the poppy family.
This term describes a short chain of amino acids joined by a particular kind of bond; string together enough of them (10,000 daltons or more) and you get a protein instead — what is it?
Peptide: Short chains of 2–50 amino acids.
Cultivated since the days of the Inca Empire and known in English as the Cape gooseberry or goldenberry, this South American nightshade now grows wild worldwide — which species is it?
Physalis peruviana: Species of cultivated South American fruit. Physalis peruviana is a species of plant in the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to Chile and Peru.

Derived from renewable resources such as corn starch and capable of biodegrading, this thermoplastic polyester made up about a quarter of the world's bioplastic market in 2022 — what compound is this?
This deciduous member of the rose family includes many varieties known as plums in English, with greengages and damsons among its subspecies — which species is it?
Prunus domestica: Species of flowering plant.

Historically nicknamed 'hydrophobia' because sufferers panic at the offer of a drink, this viral disease causes severe brain inflammation and is virtually always fatal once symptoms appear. What is it?
Rabies: Deadly viral disease, transmitted through animals.
Nicknamed golden root or Arctic root, this Crassulaceae plant is popular in herbal supplements even though the FDA has warned sellers against overselling its health benefits — which plant?
Rhodiola rosea: Species of flowering plant in the stonecrop family.
A synthetic element named for a famous physicist, it's the first of the super-heavy transactinides and behaves chemically as the heavier cousin of hafnium in group 4 — which element?
Rutherfordium: Chemical element with atomic number 104 (Rf)
Nicknamed 'Devil's Breath' and derived from nightshade plants, which motion-sickness drug has also been used historically as a deliriant?
Named for its enormous footwear-shaped beak, this large wading bird of East African swamps was once classified with storks but is now grouped with pelicans and herons — what is it?
Shoebill: Species of bird. The shoebill (Balaeniceps rex), also known as the whale-headed stork, whalebill, and shoe-billed stork, is a large long-legged wading bird.
After designing the BBC Micro and its BASIC, this English computer scientist co-created the instruction set for ARM — now the most widely used processor architecture in smartphones. Who is she?
Common in coastal tropical waters worldwide, this group of cartilaginous fish includes about 220 species across 29 genera, from butterfly rays to manta and devil rays — what are they?

Located near the border of two constellations some 18.2 billion light-years away, this hyperluminous quasar harbors one of the most massive black holes ever found, at roughly 40 billion solar masses — what is it?
TON 618: Quasar and Lyman-alpha blob in the constellations of Canes Venatici and Coma Berenices.
Encompassing everything from storytelling to painting, this broad domain of human creative expression splits into three branches: visual, literary, and performing — what is it called?
